\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Setting and notation}
\label{sec:setup}

A floorplan is given as an occupancy map and pre-processed, as in
\cite{f3loc}, into a directional Euclidean signed distance field
$D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times O}$ on a grid of $0.1$\,m cells with
$O{=}36$ yaw bins, where $D[y,x,o]$ is the free distance from cell $(x,y)$
along bin $o$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of navigable cells.

A visual backbone maps a single image $I$ to $V$ horizontal depth rays
$\hat{\mathbf{r}} \in \mathbb{R}^{V}$, and the pose posterior is the sliding
$\ell_1$ match of those rays against $D$,
%
\begin{equation}
  p_v(y,x,o) \;\propto\; \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\,
  \big\| D[y,x,o{:}o{+}V] - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \big\|_1 \Big),
  \label{eq:visual}
\end{equation}
%
with $\lambda{=}40$. We write $\pi(c) = \max_o p_v(c,o)$ for the
position marginal and $\omega(c) = \arg\max_o p_v(c,o)$ for the yaw the
backbone prefers at cell $c$. Our method treats
\eqref{eq:visual} as a black box: we do not retrain, modify or replace the
visual model, and we evaluate on two backbones that differ in how
$\hat{\mathbf{r}}$ is produced.\footnote{UnLoc additionally predicts a per-ray
Laplace scale and divides the residual in \eqref{eq:visual} by it. Nothing in
this section depends on that choice.}

Alongside the image, a co-located loudspeaker and a six-microphone ring record a
room impulse response $g \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times N}$ at the same pose. A
candidate response $g_c$ is rendered offline at every $c \in \mathcal{C}$ from
the floorplan geometry alone. This asymmetry is deliberate and is the constraint
the method is designed around: the query is what a microphone in a furnished
room hears, while every candidate is what bare walls would produce, because bare
walls are all a deployment knows.

\subsection{Why a hypothesis-level formulation}
\label{sec:why}

The natural way to add a second modality is to combine the two scores at every
cell. We find this formulation degenerate in practice. Ranking $\pi$ over
$|\mathcal{C}| \approx 5{,}000$ cells and taking logarithms, the visual term
spans $0.009$ across the fifty cells the backbone shortlists, because all of
them lie above the $99.9$th percentile, whereas the acoustic term spans $0.67$,
a factor of $72$. A cell-wise weighted sum is therefore not a weighted sum: the
visual posterior does not participate, and the acoustic term decides alone
among the shortlist. Measured over $300$ queries, it moves the prediction on
$92\%$ of them and improves it on $52\%$, which is close to a coin flip.

The visual shortlist is also badly counted. The top fifty cells are typically
two or three distinct \emph{places}, each sampled many times, so a broad mode
outvotes a sharp one purely by cell count. Extracting places instead, ten
separated hypotheses attain the ground-truth coverage of fifty cells
($92.8\%$ against $92.3\%$) with a fifth of the candidates.

We therefore fuse at the level of spatial hypotheses.

\subsection{Spatial hypotheses}
\label{sec:hypotheses}

We extract $K{=}10$ separated modes of $\pi$ by greedy non-maximum suppression:
repeatedly take the strongest remaining cell and suppress every cell within
$\rho_{\mathrm{nms}}{=}1.5$\,m,
%
\begin{equation}
  h_k \;=\; \arg\max_{c \,\in\, \mathcal{C} \setminus \bigcup_{j<k} B(h_j)} \pi(c),
  \qquad
  B(h) = \{ c : \| c - h \|_2 \le \rho_{\mathrm{nms}} \},
  \label{eq:nms}
\end{equation}
%
and write $\mathcal{D}_k = \{c : \|c - h_k\|_2 \le \rho_{\mathrm{loc}}\}$ for a
local disc of radius $\rho_{\mathrm{loc}}{=}0.5$\,m around each hypothesis. The
suppression radius is the same separation used to define visual confidence in
Sec.~\ref{sec:gate}, so hypothesis extraction and confidence remain consistent.

Crucially, the method only ever \emph{selects} among $\{h_1,\dots,h_K\}$. The
predicted pose is $(h_{k^\star}, \omega(h_{k^\star}))$: position and yaw both
come from the visual backbone at the chosen hypothesis. Sound cannot move the
answer to a place vision did not propose, and cannot alter yaw, about which a
co-located source and receiver carry no information.

\subsection{Acoustic representation}
\label{sec:acoustic}

Each response is aligned on its direct arrival, the first $2$\,ms are discarded
so that the direct sound and any constant engine gain cancel between query and
candidate, and the following $128$\,ms are analysed. We take a short-time
spectrogram with an $n_{\mathrm{fft}}{=}256$ Hann window and hop $64$ at
$48$\,kHz, a $5.33$\,ms analysis window at $187$\,Hz resolution, and sum power
into three bands $[0,0.5), [0.5,1.5), [1.5,4)$\,kHz, giving
$\phi(g) \in \mathbb{R}^{18 \times T}$. Each row is normalised to unit sum and
concatenated with the per-row energy split, which makes $\phi$ invariant to
overall level. The acoustic score of a cell is the negative $\ell_1$ distance
%
\begin{equation}
  a(c) \;=\; -\big\| \phi(g_c) - \phi(g) \big\|_1 .
  \label{eq:score}
\end{equation}
%
The window length is not the conventional choice. Selecting it by how well sound
localises \emph{alone} favours a $2$\,ms energy envelope, and that is how it was
chosen in prior work; selecting it by how often it identifies the correct
hypothesis, which is what \eqref{eq:evidence} actually asks of it, favours the
spectrogram above by $6.3$ points (Table~\ref{tab:feature}). The two criteria
disagree, and we report both.

\subsection{Relative acoustic evidence}
\label{sec:evidence}

Sound is a weak absolute localiser here: on its own it reaches $20.7\%$ at
$1$\,m against the visual backbone's $49.7\%$. We therefore never ask it where
the query is. We ask only which of the proposed places is most consistent with
what was heard.

Each hypothesis is summarised by a robust aggregate over its disc, the $0.9$
quantile $\alpha_k = Q_{0.9}\{a(c) : c \in \mathcal{D}_k\}$, rather than by the
score at its centre. This is motivated by measurement: the ground-truth cell has
median acoustic rank $0.950$, while the best cell within $0.25$\,m has $0.992$.
The score identifies the correct region more reliably than the correct cell.

Because \eqref{eq:score} is unnormalised and its offset varies per query, we
standardise across the hypotheses of that query,
$\tilde{\alpha}_k = (\alpha_k - \mu_\alpha)/\sigma_\alpha$, and define the
evidence for a hypothesis against all the others,
%
\begin{equation}
  \varrho_k \;=\; \tilde{\alpha}_k \;-\; \log \!\!\sum_{j \neq k}\!
  \exp \tilde{\alpha}_j .
  \label{eq:evidence}
\end{equation}
%
Unlike a global percentile, \eqref{eq:evidence} is invariant to a constant shift
of the score, and it expresses exactly the comparative question sound is being
asked.

\subsection{Confidence-gated selection}
\label{sec:gate}

Sound must not overrule a confident visual prediction. We measure visual
ambiguity as the log-odds between the two strongest hypotheses and acoustic
discriminativeness as the margin of \eqref{eq:evidence},
%
\begin{equation}
  m_v = \log \pi(h_{1}) - \log \pi(h_{2}),
  \qquad
  m_a = \varrho_{(1)} - \varrho_{(2)},
  \label{eq:margins}
\end{equation}
%
where $\varrho_{(i)}$ is the $i$-th largest evidence. Both are available at
inference time and neither uses ground truth. The acoustic term is admitted
through a product of two smooth gates,
%
\begin{equation}
  \gamma \;=\; w \cdot
  \sigma\!\Big(\frac{\tau_v - m_v}{s}\Big) \cdot
  \sigma\!\Big(\frac{m_a - \tau_a}{s}\Big),
  \label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
%
and the hypothesis is chosen by
%
\begin{equation}
  k^\star \;=\; \arg\max_k \;\; \tilde{v}_k \;+\; \gamma \, \varrho_k ,
  \qquad
  \tilde{v}_k = \frac{\log \pi(h_k) - \mu_v}{\sigma_v}.
  \label{eq:select}
\end{equation}
%
Standardising both terms per query is what makes $\gamma$, $\tau_v$ and
$\tau_a$ transferable rather than scale-dependent quantities.

Setting $\gamma{=}0$ recovers the visual backbone exactly, so the method can
only be judged against a baseline it contains as a special case.

\subsection{On the two gates}
\label{sec:gates-discussion}

We report the second gate as an ablation rather than as a contribution, because
the evidence for it is weak and we prefer to say so. No acoustic
self-confidence measure we tested predicts its own correctness above
$\mathrm{AUROC}\,0.60$; the best predictor of an acoustic mistake is the
\emph{visual} quantity $m_v$, at $0.62$. Comparing the queries the acoustic term
repairs against those it breaks, the central $90\%$ of the latter contains
$98\%$ of the former by \eqref{eq:evidence}. On one backbone the tuned $\tau_a$
is $-\infty$, i.e.\ the acoustic gate is switched off, and \eqref{eq:gamma}
reduces to a gate on visual ambiguity alone.

\subsection{Implementation and protocol}
\label{sec:impl}

The structural choices, namely which summary represents a hypothesis under each
modality and the form of \eqref{eq:select}, are shared by every backbone and
selected once. The four scalars $(w, s, \tau_v, \tau_a)$ are tuned per backbone,
which is necessary because the posteriors of two backbones are on different
scales and a threshold on $m_v$ cannot mean the same thing for both.

All selection, including the acoustic feature of Sec.~\ref{sec:acoustic}, uses
the \texttt{replica\_f} pose collection; every number we report comes from the
disjoint \texttt{replica\_g} collection. Gains are reported with paired
bootstrap intervals over queries, since the two predictions for one query are
not independent.

Rendering the candidate grid is the method's main cost and is done once per
floorplan, offline: $2{,}700$ to $5{,}400$ cells per scene at $48$\,kHz. At
inference the acoustic branch is a single spectrogram and $K{=}10$ disc
aggregations, which is negligible beside the visual backbone.
